points.t: Recurrent **lip, tongue or face swelling without hives or itch** in someone on ramipril, lisinopril or another ACE inhibitor.
ACE inhibitors block **bradykinin breakdown**; bradykinin leaks fluid into deep tissue, so histamine-based treatments work poorly.
**Airway first (999)**; **stop the ACE inhibitor permanently**, record a class allergy, choose an alternative carefully.
**Airway compromise**; **hereditary angioedema**; ARB / sacubitril-valsartan cross-reactivity; gliptins add risk.

points: ACE (kininase II) normally degrades **bradykinin**; inhibition → bradykinin + substance P → **B2 receptors** → leak.
Affects ~0.1–0.7% of users; up to a third of ED angioedema.
Starts **any time: first dose to years later**.
Risk: **black ethnicity (≈3–5×)**, female, > 65, smoking, prior angioedema, **DPP-4 inhibitors**, mTOR inhibitors, **sacubitril / valsartan** (contraindicated within 36 h of ACE-i), alteplase.
Triggers: minor trauma, surgery, dental work, intubation.

visuals.caption: Histamine angioedema (left): mast cells release histamine, giving itchy surface wheals. Bradykinin angioedema (right): deep vessel leak with smooth swelling and no wheals, so antihistamines don’t help.
visuals.alt: Two skin cross-sections: mast-cell wheal versus deep bradykinin leak

points: Face, periorbital, **lips, tongue**, floor of mouth, larynx; gut attacks (abdominal pain).
**No urticaria**, poor response to antihistamine / steroid.
Attacks may recur **for weeks after stopping** (wanes over ~1–3 months): not treatment failure.

visuals.caption: Angioedema: deep swelling of lips and eyelids. When it comes without wheals in someone on an ACE inhibitor, think bradykinin.
visuals.alt: Face with swollen lips and eyelids

points: Angioedema, **no wheals**, on an ACE-i, no antihistamine response.
If no ACE-i, family history, onset < 40, or recurrence after stopping (HAE / AAE: C4 low).

cards.name: Histamine angioedema
cards.clue: Wheals / itch, minutes, < 24 h, responds to antihistamine / adrenaline.

cards.name: Hereditary / acquired C1-INH deficiency
cards.clue: Low C4; family history; acquired → look for lymphoproliferative disease.

points: **Stop the ACE-i permanently**: record “ACE inhibitor: angioedema (class reaction), avoid all ACE inhibitors”. No rechallenge. **Yellow Card**.
Explain swelling may recur for several weeks.
**ARB with caution** (recurrence ~2–10%): discuss, consider specialist advice, safety-net.
Or a **calcium-channel blocker** (amlodipine) ± SGLT2 inhibitor for renal protection.
Stop antihistamine / prednisolone that gave no benefit (steroid harm, e.g. hyperglycaemia).
Airway management; adrenaline if anaphylaxis can’t be excluded; off-label icatibant / C1-INH / FFP (mixed evidence).

items.t: Tongue / throat swelling, voice change, stridor, difficulty swallowing: **999**.
Recurrent angioedema without ACE-i or with family history; abdominal attacks; > 3 months after stopping: **immunology** (C4 / C1-INH).

pearls.t: Angioedema **without wheals** on an ACE-i = bradykinin. Antihistamines won’t fix it; **stopping the ACE-i** will (eventually).
Medication review: ask every ACE-i patient about past face or tongue swelling.
Risk persists for years, not just the first month.

quiz.a: ACE inhibition blocks bradykinin breakdown (not histamine / IgE).

quiz.q: Swelling recurs 2 weeks after stopping ramipril: treatment failure?
quiz.a: No: attacks can recur for weeks–months.

quiz.q: Which combination drug is contraindicated within 36 h of an ACE-i?
Test if no ACE-i and family history?
